title: Eating for a Sustainable Planet: Personalized Sustainable Diet Recommendation via Constraint-Aware Decision-Making Modeling
one_liner: The paper recommends meals by treating sustainability as explicit constraints and personal taste as the thing to optimize inside those limits, so better planetary choices do not depend on pretending people directly prefer them.
lead: Diet recommendation is not a one-number problem. A meal plan should satisfy nutrition, cost, cultural fit, and environmental impact at the same time. Population-level studies can say what a sustainable diet should look like on average, but an individual recommender must still respect what a person is willing to eat. This paper separates those roles. It treats personal preference as the objective to maximize, while sustainability enters as learnable constraints that define which choices are acceptable. That lets the system search for meals a person is likely to adopt without abandoning the broader sustainability requirements.

problem.h2: Why sustainable diet advice is hard at the individual level
paras: A sustainable diet must satisfy several requirements at once. The meals should nourish the person, stay affordable, fit their habits, and reduce environmental burden. Many recommendation systems treat all of those concerns as if they were just more user preferences. That is risky because a person may prefer meals that violate nutrition or sustainability limits.

The paper argues that sustainability should not be modeled only as a taste signal. Instead, sustainability should define what is allowed, while the recommender uses personal preference to choose among the allowed options.

callout.html: Do not ask the model to guess that users secretly prefer sustainability. Put sustainability into the decision constraints and optimize preference inside those bounds.

panels.title: 1. Many goals collide
panels.caption: A diet plan has to satisfy several dimensions at once.

panels.title: 2. Preference-only modeling fails
panels.viz_args: user likes it, but diet target is broken
panels.caption: A purely preference-driven system can recommend meals that the user enjoys but that fail sustainability or nutrition requirements.

panels.title: 3. Learn feasible limits
panels.caption: The system learns how tight each requirement should be from data rather than relying on one fixed hard rule.

panels.title: 4. Search inside the feasible set
panels.caption: Recommendations come from the set that respects the learned constraints.

panels.title: 5. Pick the preferred option
panels.caption: Among feasible meals, the system chooses the one most likely to match the person.

steps.text: Use the SusDiet collection so the system has recipes with measured nutrition, cost, culture-related properties, and environmental indicators.
Learn which meals each person is more likely to accept from interaction history or preference signals.
Represent the four sustainability pillars as constraints whose strength can be learned from data, because different settings may require different tradeoffs.
Keep only recommendations that satisfy the learned constraint set.
Among the acceptable options, recommend the meals the user is most likely to choose.

paras: The paper changes the decision rule from preference-only ranking to constrained decision making, where personal taste is optimized inside a sustainability-feasible set.
object.object: the rule that turns user preference and meal attributes into final recommendations

hidden.name: the feasible region where a meal is both sustainable enough and personally acceptable
paras: The hidden quantity is the feasible region of meals that satisfy the sustainability requirements while still remaining plausible choices for the individual. A recommendation is only useful if it falls inside that region. Too strict a constraint set can remove nearly everything the user will accept, while too loose a set lets unsustainable options through.

The paper learns this region instead of fixing it by hand. That matters because the practical decision is not to maximize sustainability alone or preference alone. It is to choose the best meal from the set that respects both.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark meals that survive the sustainability screen and still have a realistic chance of adoption.

reads.html: The important question is which meals are both acceptable enough for the user and good enough for the planet, because recommendations outside that overlap will fail in practice.
The method learns a sustainability-feasible decision region and then optimizes personal preference within that region.

mechanism.h2: Why constraints help more than pretending sustainability is a preference
paras: If the system treats sustainability as just another taste feature, it can decide that a user's immediate preference outweighs the diet requirements. That gives high click or acceptance scores but poor real-world sustainability. Constraint-aware decision making avoids that failure because the model first determines which meals are acceptable under the sustainability pillars.

The learned constraints matter because real settings differ in how tight each pillar should be. Once the feasible set is formed, preference ranking becomes useful again because it chooses the option the user is most likely to adopt among the meals that already satisfy the broader requirements.

stages.s: user signals and recipe sustainability features

math.h2: Maximize preference subject to sustainability limits
math.words: Choose the meal with the highest predicted user preference among those that satisfy the learned nutrition, affordability, cultural, and environmental constraints.
math.equation: meal^* = argmax_m pref(user, m) subject to c_k(m) <= tau_k for all k
symbols: the predicted preference score of the user for meal m
the value of meal m on sustainability requirement k
the learned allowable limit for sustainability requirement k
one of the four sustainability pillars

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Meal A has preference score 9 but fails the environmental limit.
Meal B has preference score 8 and satisfies all four limits.
Meal C has preference score 7 and also satisfies all four limits.
Meal A is removed because it violates a constraint.
Meal B is chosen because it is the most preferred option inside the feasible set.

math.note: The paper's learned constraints can be more flexible than fixed thresholds, but the decision structure is exactly this: optimize taste inside a sustainability-feasible set.

charts.title: Preference-only recommenders
charts.note: These systems can please users in the short term, but they fail the broader diet mission because nothing stops them from recommending unsustainable meals.

charts.title: Constraint-aware recommender
charts.note: The paper reports better sustainability without sacrificing too much user fit because the model searches for the best acceptable meal rather than the unconstrained favorite.

items.b: The learned constraints can be miscalibrated.
items.html: If the constraint strengths are set too loosely, unsustainable meals slip through, and if they are set too tightly, the system may recommend meals that users reject because the feasible set is too narrow.

items.b: Preference signals may reflect short-term habit only.
items.html: If the model learns from very narrow past choices, it can underestimate meals the user would accept after small guidance because it only sees current habit.
If some cuisines or affordability bands are underrepresented, the recommender may struggle to find feasible meals for those groups because the candidate pool itself is biased.
The method works when the recipe pool is broad and the sustainability limits are well learned, because then the model can offer realistic meals that satisfy the full decision problem.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small meal recommendation sandbox with recipes labeled by calories, nutrient balance, cost, cuisine tag, and carbon estimate. Simulate a few users with different taste profiles. Compare an unconstrained ranking model with a constraint-aware recommender that first filters by sustainability rules and then ranks by preference.

The demo should show higher sustainability compliance with only limited loss in acceptance because the constraint-aware system recommends the best meal inside a feasible set instead of recommending the overall favorite regardless of impact.
demo.closing: The decisive result is more accepted recommendations that satisfy all four pillars, because that is the practical definition of a sustainable personalized diet system.
